dimension: Scheduling and resource-allocation theory for heterogeneous machines
citations_that_failed: MISATTRIBUTED: 'Zhou, Shroff, Wierman, arXiv:2003.02368'. arXiv:2003.02368 is 'LSQ: Load Balancing in Large-Scale Heterogeneous Systems with Multiple Dispatchers' by Shay Vargaftik, Isaac Keslassy and Ariel Orda (cs.NI, 4 Mar 2020). The Zhou/Shroff/Wierman paper, 'Asymptotically Optimal Load Balancing in Large-scale Heterogeneous Systems with Multiple Dispatchers', is arXiv:2002.08908 (20 Feb 2020). The substantive point survives (LSQ's abstract does state JSQ(d) and JIQ are 'either unstable or perform poorly'), but the identifier and the author list do not match.

ASSUMPTION MISSTATED: 'TIGHT bounds per m approaching e/(e-1), about 1.58, when bags equal machines' attributed to Eberle, Hoeksma, Megow, Noelke, Schewior, Simon (arXiv:2011.05181). The abstract of that paper gives 2 - 1/m in the general setting, 1.8 for equal-size jobs, 4/3 as a lower bound for equal-size jobs, and e/(e-1) as the OPTIMAL factor for INFINITESIMAL jobs ('sand'). The qualifier is infinitesimal jobs, not bags equal machines. Minarik and Sgall (arXiv:2407.11670) subsequently give 1.6 for equal-size jobs at b = m, improving 1.8, against a previous lower bound of 1.58 -- so at b = m the figure is an unmatched lower bound, not a tight bound.

OBJECTIVE/MODEL TRANSFER INVALID: Duerr, Erlebach, Megow, Meissner (ITCS 2018, LIPIcs 94; full version arXiv:1709.02592) is cited as independent corroboration that measurement can recover at most about 58% to 100%. Verified from the full text: Theorem 21 gives phi approx 1.618 as the optimal DETERMINISTIC ratio and Theorem 22/23 give 4/3 randomized, for scheduling with testing to minimise MAKESPAN on a SINGLE machine, where testing costs 1 time unit and reveals a JOB's processing time. phi is the ratio of an algorithm that DOES test, versus an omniscient optimum. In that model an algorithm that never tests is unboundedly bad (ratio p_bar/p). The paper therefore says the prize from measurement is unbounded, not bounded by 1.618. It is not a second, independent confirmation of the 1.58-to-2 claim.

INCOMPLETE ATTRIBUTION (minor, not a failure of existence): 'Minarik, arXiv:2407.11670' omits co-author Jiri Sgall. 'Deng, Journal of Educational Measurement 47(2):202-226, 2010' omits co-authors Timothy Ansley and Hua-Hua Chang; the paper exists under the title 'Stratified and Maximum Information Item Selection Procedures in Computer Adaptive Testing'. 'Gardner, Jaleel, Wickeham, Doroudi, Performance Evaluation, 2020' is indexed as Performance Evaluation 145:102151 (2021); 2020 is the conference version.

UNCITED LOAD-BEARING CLAIM: 'it has already been applied to language-model evaluation' (item response theory for LLM evaluation) carries no citation at all, yet it is one of the two pillars of the 'wheel is already invented' verdict for the cold-start probe. Pandora's box is likewise invoked with no citation to Weitzman (1979). Candidate citations exist (Lalor et al. 2016; Rodriguez et al. ACL 2021; Polo et al., tinyBenchmarks, ICML 2024) but none was given and none was verified in this session.

NOT RE-VERIFIED IN THIS SESSION (no reason to doubt, flagged for completeness): Lenstra/Shmoys/Tardos Math Prog 46:259-271 1990 exact page range (corroborated only indirectly, via secondary sources that cite [LST90] as the rounding giving ratio 2); Mitzenmacher TPDS 11(1):6-20 exact volume and pages (PODC 1997 origin and the substantive finding both confirmed via the author's own abstract page); van der Linden and Glas (Springer 2000); Raman/Livny/Solomon HPDC 1998; Ousterhout/Wendell/Zaharia/Stoica SOSP 2013; Mukhopadhyay and Mazumdar. Web search budget for the turn was exhausted before these could be closed out.
quantitative_errors: The 37% probe-budget threshold is derived from the wrong end of the dimension's own stated range. 1 - 1/1.5820 = 0.3679, which is exactly 1/e, and 1.58 is the infinitesimal-jobs figure. The founder's roster is 1 to 700, where the general speed-robust bound is 2 - 1/700 = 1.9986, giving 1 - 1/1.9986 = 0.4996. On the dimension's own logic the cap is about 50%, not 37% -- it understates the permissible probe budget by about a third. The derivation also mixes units, converting a makespan ratio directly into a fraction of 'the experiment's budget', and is presented as holding 'by construction'.

'One-shot binding squares your measurement error' does not follow from Theorem 1.2. Verified from the PDF: (i) clairvoyant 8mu, (ii) clairvoyant non-preemptive 7.216mu^2, (iii) non-clairvoyant 108mu. Distortion is mu = mu_1 * mu_2 with mu_1 = max(s_hat/s) and mu_2 = max(s/s_hat), so mu >= 1 always. 7.216mu^2 < 8mu for every mu < 8/7.216 = 1.1086, i.e. the non-preemptive bound is numerically BETTER at and near perfect prediction. These are two UPPER bounds proved for two DIFFERENT algorithms; no lower bound separating preemptive from non-preemptive is cited, so no penalty for one-shot binding is established at all.

Theorem 1.4(i)'s constant 216 is treated as a working guarantee at the founder's scale. With m between 1 and 700, 216-competitive is operationally vacuous for any roster below a few hundred machines, and at m = 700 it beats the Omega(m) lower bound by roughly a factor 3 (with the hidden constant in Omega(m) unspecified). The claim that mechanism 3 is 'the single most useful result for CDSFL' is not supported by the magnitude of its constant.

Mechanism 3's summary sentence, 'An ordinal ranking is enough for constant-competitive scheduling', drops the machine model. Verified: Theorem 1.3 (at most 8) and Theorem 1.4(i) (at most 216) are both for speed-ordered RELATED machines. For speed-ordered UNRELATED machines Theorem 1.4(ii) is Theta(log min{n, m}) -- not constant. The dimension itself declares unrelated machines the correct formalisation in mechanism 1, so its own headline is inconsistent with its own framing.

Mechanism 5's description of Iterative Greedy as 'the free machine i with the largest estimated speed s_ij' is slightly off: Algorithm 6 of the paper takes arg max over (i, j) of w_j * s_hat_ij, i.e. weight times predicted speed, and the Omega(n) bound in Lemma C.1 is stated for unit weights. Immaterial to the conclusion, but the rule is a density rule, not a pure speed rule.

Mechanism 5's 'worst proven guarantee in the whole set' needs the objective qualifier. Lemma C.1's Omega(n) is in the number of JOBS for total completion time. For MAKESPAN on unrelated machines, greedy is exactly m-competitive (Aspnes, Azar, Fiat, Plotkin, Waarts, JACM 44(3):486-504, 1997), i.e. bounded in n. Which greedy is worse depends on the objective, and the dimension declared the objective to be makespan.
overstated_verdicts: Mechanism 2 (Observation 1.1), DIRECTLY_APPLICABLE: the observation is verified verbatim but is for 'minimizing the total (weighted) completion time on m related machines'. The dimension's own mechanism 1 declares the objective to be R||Cmax (makespan). The makespan analogue in that paper is the informal Section 1.1 example (m time units blind versus immediate with knowledge), not Observation 1.1. The verdict should be APPLICABLE_WITH_CHANGES with the objective substitution named.

Mechanism 3 (speed-ordered machines), DIRECTLY_APPLICABLE: the paper's speed-ordered model requires s_ij >= s_i'j if and only if i <= j for ALL jobs j -- a single global order valid across every claim, with only the magnitudes job-dependent. The dimension's own heterogeneity note concedes this is likely false for CDSFL. A verdict of DIRECTLY_APPLICABLE on a model whose defining assumption the same entry says is violated is internally inconsistent.

Mechanism 3 and 4, against the no-central-coordinator hard constraint: Algorithms 1 to 5 in the paper all compute assignments over the full machine and job sets at each decision point (the clairvoyant one maximises total predicted density across a feasible job-to-machine assignment). None is decentralised. Every scheduling-theory guarantee cited in this dimension assumes a single dispatcher holding global state, and no mechanism verdict records that. The decentralisation constraint is handled only by the systems citations (Condor, Sparrow, BOINC), none of which carries a competitive bound.

Mechanism 4 (migration necessity), DIRECTLY_APPLICABLE, used to issue the hard design ruling that tiers must be revisable 'per claim, not per experiment': the theorem's model presumes partial progress is transferable, since a job's remaining processing requirement carries over when it moves. If a CDSFL work unit is atomic (a verification call either completes or is discarded), migration in the theorem's sense is not implementable and the applicable model is non-preemptive or restart-based, with different bounds. The interface assumption was not tested before the ruling was issued.

Claim 2 of the disagreement section ('the routing policy his tiering implies is the single worst-guaranteed policy in the set'): Mitzenmacher's result is cited as reaching 'the same conclusion', but it concerns STALE queue-length information in a homogeneous large-system limit, not heterogeneous capability estimates, and its remedy (choose the lighter of 2 randomly sampled servers) is precisely the policy that Gardner et al. show can destabilise a heterogeneous system with concentrated capacity. The two supporting citations in claims 2 and 4 pull in opposite directions and the dimension does not reconcile them.

missed_mechanisms.name: Online load balancing on unrelated machines (exponential-potential assignment): O(log m)-competitive makespan with immediate, irrevocable dispatch
missed_mechanisms.citation: J. Aspnes, Y. Azar, A. Fiat, S. Plotkin, O. Waarts, 'On-line routing of virtual circuits with applications to load balancing and machine scheduling', Journal of the ACM 44(3):486-504, May 1997 (earlier: STOC 1993, 'On-line load balancing with applications to machine scheduling and virtual circuit routing'). https://cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/papers/stoc93-abstract.html
missed_mechanisms.why_it_matters: This is the canonical online result for exactly the dimension's declared objective and machine model -- makespan on unrelated machines, where each job's load increment depends on both job and machine, and each job must be assigned immediately on arrival. It is O(log m)-competitive and NON-MIGRATORY, and the paper proves the natural greedy is exactly m-competitive. Its absence is the largest single hole: it falsifies the migration mandate on the makespan objective (you do not need migration for a polylog guarantee, you need the right potential function), it gives a decentralisable rule that fits the no-central-coordinator constraint far better than migration does, and it shows the fix for greedy is known and constructive rather than a dead end. The dimension instead imports Omega(m) and Omega(n) results proved only for total completion time and issues makespan-framed design rulings from them.

missed_mechanisms.name: Work stealing: decentralised migration with provable bounds
missed_mechanisms.citation: R. D. Blumofe and C. E. Leiserson, 'Scheduling multithreaded computations by work stealing', Journal of the ACM 46(5):720-748, 1999; heterogeneous extension in M. A. Bender and M. O. Rabin, 'Online scheduling of parallel programs on heterogeneous systems with applications to Cilk', Theory of Computing Systems 35(3):289-304, 2002. NOT verified in this session -- the turn's web search budget was exhausted; treat the volume and page numbers as unconfirmed.
missed_mechanisms.why_it_matters: The dimension asserts two constraints that it never reconciles: migration is mandatory (mechanism 4) and there is no central coordinator. Work stealing is the one mechanism family that satisfies both, because migration happens by idle-worker pull with no global state and no dispatcher. Its guarantees are stated in the form the founder needs (expected completion in T1/P plus a term in the critical-path length), a starved worker pulls work rather than being told to, and a demoted worker is never idle-by-construction -- which is exactly the 'reassigned, not deleted' property the dimension says must be enforced. Condor matchmaking, Sparrow and BOINC are all push or pull DISPATCH mechanisms; none of them migrates work already in flight, so the dimension's decentralisation half and its migration half are currently answered by disjoint, mutually incompatible citations.

missed_mechanisms.name: Online scheduling with predicted machine capability (learning-augmented makespan)
missed_mechanisms.citation: S. Lattanzi, T. Lavastida, B. Moseley, S. Vassilvitskii, 'Online Scheduling via Learned Weights', SODA 2020, pp. 1859-1877. NOT verified in this session (search budget exhausted); treat page numbers as unconfirmed.
missed_mechanisms.why_it_matters: This is the makespan counterpart to Theorem 1.2's completion-time predictions: restricted assignment where predicted machine weights replace exact capability, with error-dependent guarantees. It is the direct formal answer to 'measure capability imperfectly, then schedule against the estimate' under the dimension's own stated objective, and it is the natural place to price the probe against the schedule. Omitting it leaves the dimension's central gap claim ('nobody has solved paying a per-probe cost to learn entries of an m-by-n matrix then scheduling against it') resting on a narrower literature review than a specialist would accept.

notes:
VERDICT RATIONALE. The five mechanism entries are, individually, accurate and honestly cited -- unusually so. The failure is concentrated in the STRONGEST DISAGREEMENT section, whose headline claim is unsound, and in one misattributed arXiv identifier.

WHAT WAS CHECKED HOW. The ICML 2023 paper (Lindermayr, Megow, Rapp, PMLR 202) carries 4 of 5 mechanisms, so I pulled the PDF and extracted the text with pdftotext rather than relying on a summary. Every theorem number, constant, machine model and objective claimed for it is correct, and two quoted sentences are verbatim: 'We show in Appendix C that Iterative Greedy is not competitive (lower bound of Omega(n))' and 'Iterative Greedy performs best among the non-clairvoyant algorithms, but does not offer any theoretical guarantees'. Theorem 3.1 reads 'Any non-migratory speed-oblivious algorithm has a competitive ratio of at least Omega(m) for minimizing the total completion time on m speed-ordered machines, even if it is clairvoyant and the machines are related' -- as claimed. I also verified BOINC adaptive replication at '(host, app version)' granularity from the full text of arXiv:1903.01699, and the golden-ratio and 4/3 results from the full text of arXiv:1709.02592 (Theorems 21 and 22). Eberle et al., Minarik and Sgall, Albers and Eckl, Zhou/Shroff/Wierman and Vargaftik et al. were checked on their arXiv abstract pages; Shchepin and Vakhania, Gardner et al., Mitzenmacher, Deng/Ansley/Chang and Aspnes et al. by targeted search of bibliographic records and author pages. Arithmetic (1/e, the 7.216 crossover at mu = 1.1086, 2 - 1/m at m = 700) was computed, not estimated.

THE ONE THING TO FIX FIRST. Disagreement claim 1 is the stated answer to 'how does my idea stack up' and it fails in three independent ways: the 1.58 figure's assumption is infinitesimal jobs rather than bags-equal-machines; speed-robust scheduling is on uniformly related machines, one speed scalar each, whereas the dimension's own mechanism 1 declares unrelated machines the correct formalisation and under job-dependent capability blind commitment is not bounded by 2 at all (the ICML paper's own Section 1.1 example gives m time units blind versus immediate with knowledge); and the golden ratio is not independent corroboration, since in that model an algorithm that never tests is unboundedly bad, so that literature says the prize from measurement is UNBOUNDED. The derived budget cap then uses 1.58 rather than the 2 - 1/m that applies at a 700-model roster, understating the permissible probe budget by about a third (50% rather than 37%).

WHAT SURVIVES INTACT, AND IS WORTH KEEPING. Mechanism 4's reading of the migration theorem is correct as stated and does contradict static tiering on the completion-time objective. Mechanism 5 is a genuine falsification of greedy best-machine routing and the paper's own empirical result (greedy wins in practice, with no guarantee) is reported honestly rather than suppressed -- that tension is the most useful single fact in the dimension. The observation that the bracket's output need only be an ORDER, not a calibrated magnitude, is correct for related machines and is the right design simplification to keep. The claim that nobody has priced per-probe learning of an m-by-n capability matrix jointly with scheduling against it was not refuted by anything I found, though the three missed mechanisms narrow the gap.

ONE CROSS-CUTTING GAP NO MECHANISM OWNS. Every competitive bound cited in this dimension assumes a single dispatcher with global state. The founder's no-central-coordinator constraint is answered only by Condor, Sparrow and BOINC, none of which carries a competitive guarantee, and none of which migrates in-flight work. The migration mandate and the decentralisation constraint are therefore currently supported by disjoint and mutually incompatible citation sets. Work stealing is the one family that closes both at once.
